about.title: Portola Valley Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Portola Valley's rural roads and wooded properties come with uneven walkways, gravel driveways, and poorly lit trails that can turn an ordinary visit into a serious injury. Whether the fall happened at a business along Alpine Road, a private event off Portola Road, or a rental property near Westridge Drive, California law puts the responsibility on property owners and managers to keep their premises reasonably safe. That means fixing known hazards or warning visitors about them. If you were hurt because a property owner ignored a broken step, wet floor, or hidden hazard, an independent attorney in our network can review what happened and explain your options. LawProactive doesn't practice law or charge fees ourselves — we simply make the introduction. From there, the attorney works on contingency, meaning there's no cost to you unless your claim results in a recovery. Acting soon matters, since evidence like surveillance footage can disappear quickly.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney About a Portola Valley Fall

items.title: Proving the Property Owner Knew
items.desc: California requires showing the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to fix or warn about it. An attorney can help gather maintenance records, prior complaints, or inspection logs to establish that notice.

items.title: Preserving Surveillance Footage Before It's Gone
items.desc: Many properties overwrite security video within days or weeks. Acting quickly to request and preserve footage can be critical to showing what actually happened.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you may still recover a reduced amount. An attorney can help present the facts fairly rather than let blame get assigned unfairly.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip and fall claim in Portola Valley?
items.answer: Generally, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If the property involved is owned by a government entity, that window is much shorter, so it's worth checking your situation early.

items.question: What if I fell on a private trail or unincorporated property near Portola Valley?
items.answer: San Mateo County includes many private and semi-rural properties, and ownership can affect how a claim is handled. An independent attorney can help identify who's responsible and what evidence to gather.

items.question: Do I need to prove the property owner was careless?
items.answer: You generally need to show the owner knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix or warn about it in time. Documenting the condition with photos and witness information right after the fall can make this easier to establish later.
